title: OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection
subtitle: How a resource server turns an opaque access token into a yes/no verdict — a back-channel call you won't see in the browser (RFC 7662).

steps.label: Call the API with an opaque token
steps.lede: The client presents its access token as a Bearer credential. Note the token is opaque — not a JWT — so there is nothing to base64url-decode; its meaning is resolved only by introspection.
steps.devtools: In the Network tab, filter on your API host (api.example.com). Read the Authorization: Bearer header. Try to decode it — you can't: an opaque token has no .-delimited parts. Only this hop is browser-visible; the introspection call is next and happens server-side.

steps.label: POST /introspect
steps.lede: The resource server asks the authorization server what the token means. It authenticates with its OWN client credentials (HTTP Basic) — this is machine-to-machine and never appears in a browser Network tab.
steps.devtools: Not in the browser — reproduce it from the resource server or read AS access logs filtered on /introspect. The Basic value decodes to rs-orders:rs-s3cr3t-shhh, the resource server's own identity. Never log the secret in production.

steps.label: 200 active:true + claims
steps.lede: The AS looks up the token, confirms it is neither expired nor revoked, and returns its metadata: scope, subject, audience, expiry, and a cnf confirmation because this token is sender-constrained (DPoP-bound).
steps.devtools: active is the canonical verdict — everything downstream hinges on it. Convert exp with date -u -d @1774000000. A cnf.jkt means the token is bound to a DPoP key: the API must ALSO verify the presented proof's thumbprint matches. See the DPoP flow.

steps.label: Enforce the verdict
steps.lede: The resource server runs its checklist against the response before returning any data. This is where the token is actually authorized for this specific call.
steps.code:
active === true                       → else 401 invalid_token
aud === "https://api.example.com"     → reject a token for another API
"read:orders" in scope                → required scope present
exp (1774000000) in the future       → token still live
cnf.jkt present                       → also verify DPoP proof thumbprint
steps.devtools: No network event. A resource server MUST NOT fail open: if any check fails, reject. If cnf.jkt is present but no matching DPoP proof accompanied the request, that is a rejection too.

steps.label: 200 data
steps.lede: All checks passed, so the resource server returns the protected payload.
steps.devtools: Back in the browser Network tab, the /resource request now shows a 200 with the payload. The whole introspection round-trip that authorized it was invisible from here.

steps.label: Inactive token → 401
steps.lede: When the token is expired, revoked, or unknown, introspection returns exactly {"active":false} — no other claims. The API turns that into a 401.
steps.devtools: RFC 7662 §2.2: an inactive token echoes only active:false — never scope, sub, or exp — so it can't be used as an information-leak oracle. The API responds 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token".

steps.label: Cache the positive result
steps.lede: A resource server may cache active:true metadata up to exp and skip /introspect on later calls. In logs this shows as a resource call with no matching introspection round-trip.
steps.devtools: The trade-off: caching trades a revocation-detection delay for latency. TTL is bounded by exp. Until the cache expires, a token revoked at the AS may still be honored here.
